newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi leaders slam graft as narcotics probe widens.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi leaders slam graft as narcotics probe widens.

text.p: Vietnam's Communist Party leaders have stepped up their war of words against the scourge of corruption and slammed the loss of revolutionary fervour within party ranks, official media reports said on Thursday.

The leadership's new offensive came amid reports from the official Vietnam News that at least nine military and police officials had now been arrested for their alleged involvement in a huge drug-trafficking racket.

The Hanoi police department's investigation bureau declined to comment on the reports which said one captain and two senior lieutenants of the Border Guard Command were detained last week, taking the number arrested in connection with the case to 31.
At least two police officers, one of them from the anti-drugs squad, had already been arrested on evidence from the death-row confession of a convicted Laotian drugs trafficker.

The Laotian, who won a stay of execution after breaking down in front of the firing squad, was reported to have unveiled a cross-border network of dealing in heroin from the notorious Golden Triangle on the borders of Thailand, Burma and Laos.
Party Secretary General Do Muoi, speaking at a conference on internal security, warned that moral degeneration among officials had opened a flank for enemies to sabotage the revolution.

The party daily, Nhan Dan, quoted him as saying that decadence in official circles had "dented popular confidence in the party and become a loophole for the enemy to sabotage the revolution and distort the reputation of party and state".
Muois rail against graft was echoed by Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, a fellow member of the septuagenarian leadership troika.
Kiet told the Lao Dong journal in an interview that legal measures against corruption should be tightened and said powerful officials who were guilty of corruption should be ousted.
He said the country needed many people like "Justice Pao", the hero of a Chinese television series who metes out fair justice to common criminals and corrupt officials alike.
"Justice Pao" is hugely popular in Vietnam. Hundreds of thousands tune in to the programme twice a week and video stores do brisk business in renting out past episodes.
Last year a Hong Kong-based consultancy survey named China, Indonesia and Vietnam as Asia's most graft-ridden nations.
A recent official newspaper report said 4,900 corruption cases, causing economic losses of over $145 million, were uncovered in the first nine months of 1996 alone.

In a policy document approved at a landmark congress six months ago, the party betrayed unease about the "cult of money" that had been spawned by a decade of capitalist-style reforms and vowed to tackle "declining morality" within the party.

Political analysts say the drive to purge the party of graft is part of efforts to promote public confidence in a body whose control over the country, some leaders fear, is being quietly chipped away by foreign influences and pockets of new wealth.

The Vietnam News said on Thursday the country's first legal document aimed at curbing corruption was drafted last month and would be open for public discussion. The draft includes a suggestion that officials who siphon off 300 million dong ($27,000) or more should go in front of the firing squad or at least be imprisoned for life.
